title: Multi-Synaptic Cooperation: A Bio-Inspired Framework for Robust and Scalable Continual Learning
claim: Biologically inspired multi-synaptic connections, modulated by local activity traces, selectively activate task-relevant synapses to expand capacity across sequential tasks.
layout: 4 panels in 2x2 grid, each with a titled sub-concept; network diagram bottom-right
description: A 2x2 grid of labeled panels. (a) shows a brain icon and two neurons with branching dendrites. Three circled synaptic contacts are linked by blue arrows to a synapse cartoon. (b) compares SNN and ANN neurons. Several orange (SNN) or blue (ANN) parallel lines connect each input to a summation neuron. The SNN inputs are spike trains and the ANN inputs are numbers. (c) plots the modulation factor f_mod against eligibility strength. An input spike train and a decaying eligibility trace sit above it. Shaded bands mark potentiation (P), depression (D) and unchanged (O) regions, with arrows to |f_mod| conditions. (d) shows four task image thumbnails with orange, blue and green borders. They feed an encoding block, layered networks and a classifier. At Task T-1 the orange synapses are active. At Task T the green synapses are active and the rest are faint. The eye goes first to the colorful network in (d).
caption: Overview of the MSCN framework. (a) The phenomenon of multi-synaptic connections in biological neurons. (b) Modeling of neurons with multiple synaptic connections in both SNNs and ANNs. (c) Local synaptic activity plasticity based on eligibility traces. Depending on the eligibility trace, synapses undergo potentiation (P), depression (D), or remain unchanged (O), reflecting the modulation’s strength and direction. (d) The process of selectively activating task-relevant synapses and inhibiting irrelevant ones.
abstract: Continual learning aims to acquire new knowledge incrementally while retaining prior information, with catastrophic forgetting (CF) being a central challenge. Existing methods can mitigate CF to some extent but are constrained by limited capacity, which often requires dynamic expansion for long task sequences and makes performance sensitive to task order. Inspired by the richness and plasticity of synaptic connections in biological nervous systems, we propose the Multi-Synaptic Cooperative Network (MSCN), a generalized framework that models cooperative interactions among multiple synapses through multi-synaptic connections modulated by local synaptic activity. This design enhances model representational capacity and enables task-adaptive plasticity by means of multi-synaptic cooperation, providing a new avenue for expanding model capacity while improving robustness to task order. During learning, our MSCN dynamically activates task-relevant synapses while suppressing irrelevant ones, enabling targeted retrieval and minimizing interference. Extensive experiments across four benchmark datasets, involving both spiking and non-spiking neural networks, demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art continual learning methods with significantly improved robustness to task-order variation. Furthermore, our analysis reveals an optimal trade-off between synaptic richness and learning efficiency, where excessive connectivity can impair circuit performance. These findings highlight the importance of the multi-synaptic cooperation mechanism for achieving efficient continual learning and provide new insights into biologically inspired, robust, and scalable continual learning.
